html:
Laozi, "the Old Master", is the legendary Chinese sage held to be the author of the Tao Te Ching and the founder of Taoism. Tradition places him in the 6th century BCE, but his life is mostly legend and the dates on the chart are traditional.

The main early account is a short biography by the historian Sima Qian, written around 100 BCE, and even Sima Qian was unsure. In the traditional story:

  • He was Li Er, born in the state of Chu in the Spring and Autumn period.
  • He served as keeper of the archives at the court of the Zhou kings.
  • The young Confucius visited him to ask about ritual and came away amazed, comparing him to a dragon.
  • Tired of the decline of Zhou, he rode west on an ox. At the frontier pass the guard asked him to write down his teaching, and he left the Tao Te Ching, then vanished.

Modern scholars mostly think the book was put together by several hands over time, in the 4th century BCE, and that "Laozi" may be a name chosen to give it the weight of age.

None of this reduced his standing. He became a god in religious Taoism. The Tang dynasty, whose family name was also Li, claimed him as its ancestor. Later stories even said he had gone west to teach the Buddha.

His teaching, as the book gives it, is the opposite of Confucian effort: follow the Way, act without forcing, prefer the soft and humble to the hard and proud. Alongside Zhuangzi, it shaped Chinese art, medicine, religion and politics.
